tensions.relation: The difficulty of unsupported struggle is productive for some learners and harmful for others; the same effort that teaches one closes another.
tensions.claim_A: Engaging learners in problem-solving before instruction improves conceptual understanding and transfer.
tensions.claim_B: The same unsupported struggle produces anxiety and worse outcomes for some learners.
tensions.paper_B: Gashaj, Trninic & Formaz, When Failing Generates Math Anxiety Instead of Productivity
tensions.instance: The student with no scaffold who shuts down instead of struggling productively.
tensions.example_question: Why do I learn better when things are hard?

tensions.relation: Pushing thought out of the head — into the hand, or onto a shared surface — is what makes hard ideas learnable; two separate lines of work arrive at the same thing.
tensions.claim_A: Externalizing reasoning into bodily action (gestural replay) carries mathematical ideas into transfer.
tensions.claim_B: Externalizing reasoning into a shared representation changes what a group is able to reason about.
tensions.paper_A: Xia et al., Embodied Transfer of Mathematical Ideas Through Gestural Replay
tensions.instance: The learner who can only work a hard idea out once it is moved outside the head, into action alone, or into something a group holds in common.
tensions.example_question: Why does explaining something out loud help me understand it?

tensions.relation: The help that carries a learner through a problem is the same help that, never withdrawn, leaves them unable to begin the next one alone.
tensions.claim_A: Scaffolds and worked examples improve immediate performance and lower cognitive load.
tensions.claim_B: Fading support is what builds durable independence; support that never fades suppresses the work that learning requires.
tensions.paper_B: Wood, Bruner & Ross; Collins, Brown & Newman (scaffolding and fading)
tensions.instance: The learner who follows the worked example perfectly, then cannot begin the next problem alone.
tensions.example_question: When should I stop asking for help?

tensions.relation: What looks like a learner failing to steer themselves can be a group steering together; the competence is real but lives at the level of the group, not the person.
tensions.claim_A: Individual self-regulation and metacognitive monitoring are primary drivers of learning outcomes.
tensions.claim_B: In collaborative settings, regulatory work distributes across the group; what looks like individual failure to self-regulate may be effective shared regulation.
tensions.paper_B: Hadwin, Jarvela, Miller (socially shared regulation of learning)
tensions.instance: The student who seems unable to monitor their own progress but functions well in group work because the group is doing the monitoring.
tensions.example_question: Why do I learn better with other people than on my own?

tensions.relation: What we call being engaged names two different states — staying fixed on a task and never ceasing to question it — and they can pull in opposite directions.
tensions.claim_A: Engagement as time-on-task and behavioral persistence predicts learning outcomes.
tensions.claim_B: Engagement as cognitive depth predicts different outcomes; a learner can be behaviorally engaged but cognitively passive.
tensions.instance: The student who completes every task on time but never constructs anything new.
tensions.example_question: Why do my students seem engaged but still aren't learning?

tensions.relation: Whether a difficulty helps depends entirely on who meets it; the same technique builds durable learning in one learner and only confusion in another.
tensions.claim_A: Introducing difficulty into practice (spacing, interleaving, retrieval) impairs immediate performance but improves long-term retention and transfer.
tensions.claim_B: The same difficulties harm learners without sufficient prior knowledge, adding load and producing frustration rather than learning.
tensions.instance: Interleaved practice that produces transfer for experienced learners produces only frustration for novices using the same materials.
tensions.example_question: Why do some study techniques work for some people but not others?

tensions.relation: The mark that shows a learner where they stand is the same mark that stops them reading the guidance meant to move them forward.
tensions.claim_A: Feedback focused on forward progress improves learning by giving learners actionable information about where they are.
tensions.claim_B: The presence of grades shifts learners toward performance orientation; they read the grade rather than the guidance that came with it.
tensions.instance: The student who looks at the grade and turns the page.
tensions.example_question: Why do my students ignore my feedback?

tensions.relation: The tool that lifts a task's burden takes with it the effort that would have built the skill to do the task alone.
tensions.claim_A: Cognitive offloading tools free attention for higher-order thinking by reducing the burden of low-level operations.
tensions.claim_B: The same offloading removes the effortful processing that builds durable skill; fluency requires the practice the tool replaces.
tensions.instance: The student who writes stronger essays with assistance but cannot begin one alone.
tensions.example_question: Is using AI to help me write making me a worse writer?
